title: 1. FinTech Eco System
subtitle: Meaning · Evolution · Ecosystem players · Types · Arthashastra in FinTech
subject: FinTech

sections.heading: Introduction and Learning Objectives
sections.html:
This module lays the conceptual foundation for the entire book. It defines FinTech, traces how the field evolved, maps the ecosystem of players and their responsibilities, classifies FinTech services, weighs merits against challenges, reviews global trends and, in a distinctively Indian touch, relates the Arthashastra to modern financial governance.

Learning objectives

  • Define FinTech and explain its characteristics
  • Trace the evolution from FinTech 1.0 to 3.5
  • Identify ecosystem players and describe their roles
  • Classify FinTech services with Indian examples
  • Evaluate merits, challenges and global trends
  • Relate Arthashastra principles to FinTech applications

sections.heading: 1.1 Meaning and Definition of FinTech
sections.html:
The word FinTech is a contraction of Financial Technology. In the simplest sense it describes the application of technology to design, deliver and improve financial products and services. A broader and more useful reading, however, treats FinTech as a process of innovation rather than a list of apps: it is the continuous reshaping of how money is stored, moved, borrowed, invested and insured through software, data and networks. When a farmer in Tamil Nadu receives a subsidy directly in a bank account, when a street vendor accepts a UPI QR payment, or when a student buys a mutual fund from a phone in a few minutes, FinTech is at work.

Scholars have offered many definitions. Schueffel, after reviewing a large body of literature, described FinTech as a new financial industry that applies technology to improve financial activities [1]. The Financial Stability Board (FSB), whose definition is widely used by regulators, describes it as technology-enabled innovation in financial services that can result in new business models, applications, processes or products, with a material effect on how financial services are provided [2]. Gomber et al. emphasise that FinTech should be understood through the forces of innovation, disruption and transformation that it unleashes on incumbent institutions [3].

Why a precise definition matters

A definition is not a mere academic exercise. Regulators use it to decide who must be licensed; investors use it to decide what to fund; and students use it to decide where a topic belongs. Three features appear in nearly every serious definition: (i) technology as the enabler, such as mobile networks, cloud computing, artificial intelligence or distributed ledgers; (ii) innovation in financial services, meaning that something new is being offered or a familiar service is delivered in a fundamentally different way; and (iii) an effect on the market, either by disrupting incumbents or by being absorbed by them.

Indian example: UPI at a neighbourhood tea stall

Before 2016 a tea-stall owner in Coimbatore dealt mostly in cash. Today a printed QR code lets customers pay from any UPI app. The payment is routed through the Unified Payments Interface operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) [4], settles in seconds, and requires no card machine. This one change replaces cash handling, a bank visit for deposit and a point-of-sale terminal with a single smartphone action. It is FinTech because technology (a mobile app and a shared payment network) has changed the delivery of a financial service (a payment).

Table 1. FinTech versus traditional finance

DimensionTraditional financeFinTech
ChannelBranches, paper formsApps, web, APIs
SpeedDays for account opening or loansMinutes, often instant
Cost to serveHigh (buildings, staff)Low (automation, scale)
Data usePeriodic, document basedContinuous, analytics driven
Access hoursBanking hours24x7

Drivers of FinTech growth

FinTech did not emerge by accident; several forces converged. On the demand side, customers accustomed to seamless digital services in shopping and entertainment began to expect the same from finance, and a young, mobile-first population adopted apps quickly. On the supply side, cheaper computing, cloud services, open-source software and ubiquitous connectivity cut the cost of building financial products. The post-crisis environment after 2008 reduced trust in incumbents, tightened bank lending to small borrowers and released technical talent into new ventures [5]. Finally, public policy played a decisive role in India: Aadhaar, Jan Dhan accounts, UPI and the Account Aggregator framework created rails that start-ups could use without building them afresh.

FinTech, TechFin and digital banking

Three terms are often confused. A FinTech start-up is typically a technology-led firm that enters financial services, such as a payment app. Digital banking refers to traditional banks delivering their own services online and through apps. TechFin, a term used by Zetzsche et al., describes large technology companies that already have big data and customer relationships and extend into finance, so that finance becomes one more service on their platform [6]. The distinction matters for regulation, because the risks of a bank with a technology arm differ from those of a technology firm with a financial arm.

Table 2. Business models in FinTech

ModelDescriptionIndian illustration
Business-to-consumer (B2C)Sells directly to individualsInvestment apps, consumer lending apps
Business-to-business (B2B)Sells tools to banks and firmsPayment gateways, KYC and analytics providers
Platform or marketplaceConnects many buyers and sellers of financial productsInsurance and loan comparison platforms
Banking-as-a-ServiceProvides bank functions through APIs to other brandsPartner-bank integrations for non-bank apps
Software-as-a-ServiceSubscription software for finance functionsAccounting and invoicing tools for MSMEs

sections.heading: 1.2 Characteristics of FinTech
sections.html:
FinTech firms differ from conventional financial institutions in several recurring ways. Understanding these characteristics helps a student recognise a FinTech business model even when it is new and unfamiliar [7].

Digital-first delivery. The primary interface is a mobile app or website, not a branch. Onboarding, servicing and grievance handling are all designed for a screen. In India, the combination of low-cost smartphones, cheap mobile data and Aadhaar-based identity has made digital-first delivery realistic even in small towns.

Customer-centric design. FinTech products are built around a customer journey rather than an internal process. A good example is the single-screen UPI payment flow, which hides the complexity of banks, switches and settlement behind a PIN entry.

Speed and low cost. Automation removes manual verification, data entry and reconciliation. Because the marginal cost of serving one more customer is small, FinTechs can profitably serve segments, such as small-ticket borrowers, that banks found unviable.

Data-driven decisions. Credit scoring, fraud monitoring, pricing and marketing rely on large volumes of data and statistical models. This is why FinTech and artificial intelligence are closely linked (see Module IV).

Scalability. Cloud infrastructure and application programming interfaces (APIs) let a firm grow from thousands to millions of users without proportionate increases in cost.

Collaboration. Contrary to the popular narrative of start-ups versus banks, many successful models are partnerships: a start-up supplies the user interface and technology, while a licensed bank supplies the balance sheet and regulatory standing.

Unbundling and rebundling

A traditional bank bundles many services, such as deposits, payments, lending and advice, in one institution. FinTech tends to unbundle this package, with specialised firms excelling at one function, for example payments or investing. Later, successful firms rebundle by adding adjacent services, which is why a payment app may add loans, insurance and mutual funds. Network effects strengthen this process: the more people and merchants use a platform, the more valuable it becomes to each of them [7].

Because the marginal cost of serving another digital customer is very low, scale matters greatly. This explains the intense competition for users, large marketing spends and the pursuit of data advantage; it also explains why concentration risk can emerge in an apparently competitive market.

Key points

  • FinTech is a process of innovation, not a single product
  • Typical traits: digital-first, customer-centric, fast, data-driven, scalable and collaborative
  • Many Indian FinTechs work through bank partnerships

sections.heading: 1.3 Evolution of FinTech
sections.html:
FinTech is often thought of as a post-2010 phenomenon, but financial services have used technology for more than a century and a half. Arner, Barberis and Buckley propose a useful three-stage framework, with a further stage for emerging economies [5].

Table 3. Phases in the evolution of FinTech (after Arner et al.)

PhasePeriodDefining developments
FinTech 1.01866–1967Transatlantic telegraph cable and early electronic funds transfer made finance globally connected
FinTech 2.01967–2008ATMs, SWIFT messaging, electronic stock exchanges, online banking and core banking systems digitised the incumbent banks
FinTech 3.02008–presentAfter the global financial crisis, start-ups and technology firms entered finance with mobile payments, peer-to-peer lending, robo-advice and cryptocurrencies
FinTech 3.5Emerging economiesMobile money and public digital infrastructure leapfrogged branch networks in Asia and Africa

FinTech 1.0 (1866–1967). The laying of the first durable transatlantic cable in 1866 allowed financial information and payment instructions to cross the ocean in minutes instead of weeks. Telegraphic transfers, ticker tapes and, later, Fedwire-style systems built the plumbing of global finance [5].

FinTech 2.0 (1967–2008). The first ATM appeared in 1967. The SWIFT network (1973) standardised cross-border bank messages, and electronic exchanges such as NASDAQ replaced trading floors. In India, the 1990s and 2000s saw computerisation of bank branches, the National Stock Exchange's screen-based trading (1994), Core Banking Solutions and Internet banking. The innovators in this phase were mainly the banks themselves.

FinTech 3.0 (2008–present). The 2008 crisis damaged trust in banks and left many skilled technologists looking for new opportunities, while smartphones were spreading rapidly. New firms offered payments, loans and investments at lower cost and with better design. Bitcoin, described in a 2008 white paper [8], introduced the idea of money without a central issuer.

FinTech 3.5. In many developing economies, the key innovation was inclusion. India's JAM trinity (Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar identity and mobile phones) and the UPI payment rails are prominent examples. The World Bank's Global Findex survey shows that account ownership and digital payments have grown substantially in recent years, with India among the large contributors [9].

Fig. 1. Timeline of FinTech phases

India's FinTech journey: milestones

Table 4. Milestones in India's digital finance journey

PeriodDevelopment
1990s–2000sComputerisation of bank branches; screen-based trading on exchanges; ATMs and core banking spread
2008NPCI set up to build shared retail payment infrastructure [4]
2009–2010UIDAI created and Aadhaar enrolment begins; IMPS launched for instant interbank transfers
2014Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana launched to open basic accounts at scale
2016UPI launched; demonetisation accelerates adoption of digital payments
2019–2021RBI regulatory sandbox framework; Account Aggregator framework operationalised
2022 onwards5G rollout begins; digital rupee pilots start; digital lending norms tightened

This chronology shows a pattern: government and public institutions first created identity, accounts and payment rails; private innovators then built services on top. The sequence is often called a public rails, private innovation model and is a distinguishing feature of the Indian experience [9].

sections.heading: 1.4 The FinTech Ecosystem and Its Players
sections.html:
A FinTech ecosystem is the interconnected set of firms, institutions, regulators, investors and customers that together create, deliver and govern technology-enabled financial services. It is called an ecosystem because no single party can deliver a modern financial service alone, and the health of one participant affects the others [7], [10].

Fig. 2. Flow of a typical UPI payment through the ecosystem

Table 5. Players, roles and responsibilities

PlayerRole and responsibilityIndian examples
FinTech start-upsDesign and launch innovative products; own the customer interfaceRazorpay, Zerodha, PhonePe
Financial institutionsProvide licences, capital, deposits, trust and a large customer baseSBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank
Technology firmsSupply cloud, analytics, AI and security platformsAWS, Infosys Finacle, TCS BaNCS
Regulators and governmentFrame rules, license entities, protect consumers, ensure stabilityRBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA
Investors and venture capitalFund early-stage firms and scale-upSequoia (Peak XV), Accel
Infrastructure bodiesOperate shared payment and identity railsNPCI, UIDAI
CustomersAdopt services; supply data and feedback; bear risksIndividuals, MSMEs

Responsibilities in practice. The start-up must be innovative and compliant; the bank must open its systems through APIs without compromising security; the technology provider must guarantee uptime and data protection; and the regulator must keep rules proportionate so that innovation is not choked. Customers, too, have responsibilities: protecting credentials, verifying apps and reporting fraud promptly.

The player lifecycle: from seed to scale

A FinTech start-up typically progresses through idea and prototype, seed and early funding from angel investors or incubators, product-market fit in which a stable group of customers uses the product, growth funding from venture capital, and finally scale-up, acquisition or listing. Along the way it must secure licences or partner with licensed entities, build compliance functions and prove the unit economics of its business.

How incumbents respond: build, buy or partner

Banks and insurers can respond to FinTech competition in three ways. They can build their own digital capabilities, they can buy or invest in promising start-ups, or they can partner through APIs, white-label arrangements or joint ventures. Each option involves trade-offs between speed, control and culture. In practice, many Indian banks combine all three, building mobile apps, partnering with lending and payment platforms, and investing selectively [3].

Competition, cooperation and co-opetition

Relationships among players are not purely adversarial. A bank may compete with a payment app for customer attention yet depend on it for transaction volumes; a technology firm may supply cloud services to a bank and simultaneously offer a competing wallet. This mixture of rivalry and collaboration is called co-opetition. Regulators must therefore pay attention to dependencies and conflicts of interest, not merely to market share.

Public digital infrastructure as an ecosystem enabler

In India, infrastructure bodies such as NPCI and UIDAI act as neutral platforms. By providing common rails at low cost, they lower entry barriers for new firms and prevent any one private provider from controlling the market. Students should note that the neutrality and governance of such bodies are themselves important policy questions.

Indian example: Why the ecosystem matters in a failed payment

Suppose a UPI payment fails after the amount is debited. The cause could lie with the customer's app, the payer's bank, the NPCI switch or the payee's bank. Resolution depends on coordination: the NPCI dispute resolution mechanism, the banks' grievance channels and RBI's ombudsman scheme. Such everyday issues show why ecosystem thinking is necessary.

sections.heading: 1.5 Types of FinTech
sections.html:
FinTech services can be classified by the financial function they perform. The classification below is common in industry and academic work [11], [10].

Table 6. Major types of FinTech

TypeWhat it doesExamples
PaymentsMoves money between people and businessesPhonePe, Google Pay, Razorpay, Paytm
LendingDigital loans, peer-to-peer lending, invoice financeLendingkart, Faircent, TReDS platforms
WealthTechInvesting, advice and portfolio managementGroww, Zerodha Coin, ET Money
InsurTechOnline insurance distribution and claimsPolicyBazaar, Digit
RegTechAutomates compliance and monitoringKYC and AML software vendors
PropTechTechnology for real estate transactionsProperty portals and e-registration tools
Crypto and blockchainDigital assets and distributed ledgersCrypto exchanges, tokenisation pilots

These categories overlap. A super-app may offer payments, loans and insurance together, and a bank may use RegTech and WealthTech tools internally. Later modules examine payments and lending (Module II), wealth and crypto (Module III) and regulation (Module V) in detail.

A closer look at each type

Payments. This is the most visible category. In India it includes payment gateways and aggregators that help merchants accept online payments, prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers such as wallet providers, and third-party application providers that offer UPI apps on top of the NPCI network. Revenue may come from fees, interchange, float or cross-selling of other services.

Lending. Digital lenders use data and algorithms for underwriting and collections. Some are NBFCs with their own balance sheet; others act as technology platforms that originate loans for banks and NBFCs. The structure affects who bears credit risk and who is responsible to the borrower under RBI norms [12].

WealthTech and InsurTech. Investment apps distribute mutual funds and trade securities; insurance platforms compare policies and assist with claims. Both rely on regulated intermediaries such as SEBI-registered brokers and advisers, and IRDAI-regulated insurers and distributors.

RegTech, PropTech and crypto. RegTech helps institutions comply with KYC, AML and reporting duties. PropTech digitises property search, registration and financing. Crypto and blockchain firms provide exchanges, custody and tokenisation services, though in India they operate in an evolving legal and tax environment.

Other models. Account aggregators, credit bureaus with analytics arms and neobanks (digital-only front ends working with partner banks) are further categories that cut across the classification above.

sections.heading: 1.6 Merits and Challenges
sections.html:
Merits. The most important merit of FinTech is financial inclusion: services that were uneconomic through branches become viable through phones. Costs fall because manual processes are automated; speed rises because verification and settlement are electronic; transparency improves because every transaction leaves a digital trail; and products can be personalised using data. For small businesses, digital records created by GST and UPI can become the basis for credit.

Challenges. Each strength carries a corresponding risk. Digital trails create data privacy concerns, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is intended to address them [13]. Concentrated platforms and heavy reliance on a few cloud providers create systemic and concentration risk. Cyber-attacks and social-engineering frauds target less-aware customers. Regulatory uncertainty arises when technology outpaces law [14]. Finally, the digital divide means that people without smartphones, connectivity or literacy may be left behind, so FinTech can widen inequality if inclusion is not deliberate.

Table 7. Merits and challenges at a glance

MeritCorresponding challenge
Inclusion of the unbankedDigital divide and low literacy
Low cost and speedOperational and cyber risk
Transparency and traceabilityPrivacy and data misuse
Personalised productsAlgorithmic bias and mis-selling
Innovation and competitionRegulatory gaps and systemic risk

A risk taxonomy for FinTech

The Basel Committee has noted that fintech developments create new risks for banks and supervisors, including strategic, operational, cyber and compliance risks, and calls for stronger governance over new technologies and third-party providers [15]. It is useful to group risks as follows.

Table 8. Risk categories in FinTech

RiskDescriptionTypical mitigation
OperationalSystem outages, errors, process failuresRedundancy, testing, business continuity plans
Cyber and fraudHacking, phishing, SIM swap, social engineeringMulti-factor authentication, monitoring, customer education
Model riskWrong or biased algorithmsValidation, explainability, human oversight
Third-party riskDependence on cloud or technology vendorsDue diligence, exit plans, concentration limits
Conduct riskMis-selling, hidden fees, aggressive recoveryDisclosure rules, grievance redress, audits
Liquidity and creditRun risk on platforms, defaults on digital loansCapital buffers, prudent underwriting
Legal and complianceBreach of licensing, privacy or AML normsCompliance programmes, RegTech tools

Indian example: Common UPI frauds

Frauds in India often exploit people rather than systems: a fake 'collect request' asks the victim to enter a PIN to receive money, a doctored QR code redirects payments, or a caller posing as a bank officer extracts an OTP. Awareness that a UPI PIN is needed only to send money, never to receive it, prevents many losses.

sections.heading: 1.7 Global FinTech Trends
sections.html:
Several themes are shaping FinTech worldwide. Embedded finance places payments, credit or insurance inside non-financial apps, such as an e-commerce checkout offering instant credit. Open banking allows customers to share financial data with third parties through secure APIs, and India's Account Aggregator framework is a consent-based variant [16], [17]. Buy Now Pay Later offers short-term credit at the point of sale. Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) are digital forms of sovereign money; the Bank for International Settlements has outlined their foundational principles [18], and the Reserve Bank of India has run pilots of the digital rupee. Generative AI is being adopted for customer service, document summarisation and advisory support. Green FinTech uses data and platforms to channel capital to sustainable projects and to measure ESG performance.

Trends in the Indian context

Several global trends have local counterparts. UPI has been linked with payment systems in other countries to enable cross-border remittances and tourist payments, extending India's domestic rails abroad. The Account Aggregator network is a consent-driven form of open banking. The digital rupee pilots explore programmable and offline payments. Embedded finance is visible when e-commerce and ride-hailing apps offer credit or insurance at checkout. Generative AI is being introduced in customer service, while regulators examine its risks.

A framework to assess any trend

  • Problem solved: which customer pain point or cost does it address?
  • Enabling technology and infrastructure: what must exist for it to work at scale?
  • Economics: who pays, and is the model sustainable without subsidy?
  • Risks and regulation: what can go wrong, and who is accountable?
  • Inclusion: does it reach people who are currently excluded?

Reading the trends critically

Every trend carries trade-offs. Embedded finance improves convenience but may hide costs; open banking widens competition but raises consent and security questions; generative AI boosts productivity but needs explainability and oversight. Students should ask, for each trend: who benefits, who bears the risk and who regulates?

sections.heading: 1.8 Principles of Arthashastra in FinTech Applications
sections.html:
The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy and administration [19], [20]. Although it predates modern finance by more than two millennia, its principles of treasury protection, audit, fair dealing and public welfare map surprisingly well onto the governance challenges of digital finance.

Table 9. Arthashastra principles and FinTech parallels

PrincipleMeaningFinTech application
Kosha (treasury)A strong treasury is the foundation of the stateCyber-security, escrow accounts, custody of customer funds
Accounts and auditDetailed, supervised accountsAudit trails, immutable ledgers, automated reconciliation
Prevention of embezzlementKautilya lists many ways funds may be misappropriatedML-based fraud detection and transaction monitoring
Gudhapurusha (spies)Covert officers detect corruptionAML surveillance, anomaly detection, whistle-blower channels
Fair weights and pricesHonest measures protect traders and buyersTransparent pricing, Key Fact Statements, fair-practice codes
Yogakshema (welfare)The state secures the well-being of its peopleFinancial inclusion, Direct Benefit Transfer, grievance redress

Interpreting the parallels. Kautilya recognised that those who handle public money have both opportunity and temptation, so he advocated rotation of officers, written records and surprise inspections. Modern digital systems do the same with role-based access, logs, maker-checker controls and continuous monitoring. His emphasis on yogakshema reminds us that the ultimate test of a financial system is the welfare of ordinary people; this resonates with India's push for low-cost, interoperable public digital infrastructure.

The seven elements of the state and the FinTech ecosystem

Kautilya's saptanga theory lists seven elements of a state: the ruler (swami), ministers (amatya), territory and people (janapada), fortified capital (durga), treasury (kosha), army or enforcement (danda) and allies (mitra) [19]. The analogy below is a teaching device that helps students see a financial platform as an organisation with interdependent parts.

Table 10. Saptanga as an analogy for a FinTech platform

ElementMeaningAnalogy in a FinTech platform
SwamiLeadershipBoard and management with clear accountability
AmatyaMinisters and administratorsSkilled risk, compliance and technology teams
JanapadaPeople and territoryCustomer base and target market
DurgaFortsCyber-security architecture and infrastructure resilience
KoshaTreasuryCapital, liquidity and safeguarding of customer funds
DandaEnforcementInternal controls, audit and penalties for misconduct
MitraAlliesPartner banks, technology providers and regulators

Administration of accounts. The Arthashastra describes superintendents of departments such as the treasury, mines and trade, each required to keep detailed records and to submit them for audit. It also catalogues many ways in which officials could misappropriate funds, from under-reporting receipts to inflating expenses, and recommends deterrents including transfers of officers and surprise checks [20]. These ideas correspond to the modern controls of segregation of duties, reconciliation, audit logs and exception reporting that FinTech firms implement in software.

A caution

The comparison is a conceptual aid, not a claim that ancient practices can be applied literally. Students should use it to appreciate continuity in the logic of financial governance while relying on modern law and standards for compliance.

sections.heading: 1.9 Case Study: The UPI Ecosystem
sections.html:
Context. Before UPI, retail digital payments in India relied on cards, wallets and bank transfers that did not work smoothly across providers. Merchants faced card-machine costs, and many small transactions remained in cash. NPCI launched UPI in 2016 as an interoperable real-time payment system for account-to-account transfers using a mobile phone [4].

Stakeholders. The ecosystem includes the customer (payer), the merchant or person receiving money (payee), the payer's and payee's banks, third-party applications that provide the user interface, the NPCI switch that routes and settles transactions, and the RBI, which regulates payment systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 [21].

Table 11. Why UPI worked: design choices

Design choiceEffect
Open and interoperable standardsAny app can pay any account; customers are not locked in
Virtual payment address and QRPayments without sharing account details
Two-factor authentication (device plus PIN)Security suited to mobile use
Real-time settlement, low or zero cost to usersRapid adoption by small merchants and individuals
Layered on Aadhaar and Jan Dhan accountsWide base of accounts to connect

Challenges. UPI has to manage fraud, system capacity during peak days, concentration of volumes among a few apps, and questions about how a free-to-user service can sustain its costs. Lessons. Public rails with open participation can create competition and scale; trust is built through reliability and recourse; and sustainability requires a clear economic model alongside inclusion goals.

Indian example: Festival-season peaks

During festival shopping seasons, transaction volumes spike. Banks and NPCI plan capacity, monitor failures and issue advisories so that payments for small traders and customers remain smooth, illustrating how ecosystem coordination works in practice.

Discussion

If UPI is free for users, who should bear the cost of running it? How can the system avoid dependence on a handful of apps?

sections.heading: Chapter Summary
sections.html:
Chapter summary

  • FinTech is technology-enabled innovation in financial services, not merely a set of apps
  • It evolved through telegraph, ATM and SWIFT, post-crisis start-up and inclusion-led phases
  • Start-ups, banks, technology firms, regulators, investors, infrastructure bodies and customers form an interdependent ecosystem
  • Merits such as inclusion and speed are matched by privacy, cyber and systemic risks
  • Arthashastra's themes of treasury, audit and welfare remain relevant to digital finance

sections.heading: Review Questions
sections.html:
The questions follow the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create); the level is shown in italics after each question. Answer each in your own words, using the module and the Indian examples.

Short answer questions

  1. Define FinTech and state any two characteristics that distinguish it from traditional finance. (Remember)
  2. List the four phases in the evolution of FinTech with their approximate periods. (Remember)
  3. Name any four players in the FinTech ecosystem and state one responsibility of each. (Remember)
  4. Explain the difference between a FinTech start-up, digital banking and TechFin. (Understand)
  5. Explain the concepts of unbundling and rebundling in FinTech with a suitable example. (Understand)
  6. Describe the role of public digital infrastructure in the growth of FinTech in India. (Understand)
  7. A tea-stall owner in a small town wants to shift from cash to digital payments. Identify the type of FinTech service involved and the ecosystem players who participate in one transaction. (Apply)
  8. Classify the following incidents under the risk categories of FinTech and justify your classification: a UPI collect-request scam, a cloud service outage and a biased loan-scoring algorithm. (Apply)
  9. Explain how Kautilya's concept of kosha relates to the safeguarding of customer funds in a digital platform. (Understand)
  10. Distinguish between the merits and the challenges of FinTech with reference to financial inclusion. (Analyse)

Long answer questions

  1. Trace the evolution of FinTech through the phases proposed by Arner, Barberis and Buckley, and analyse how the innovators and technologies differ in each phase. (Analyse)
  2. Analyse the FinTech ecosystem by describing the roles and responsibilities of each player and the relationships of cooperation, competition and co-opetition among them. (Analyse)
  3. Examine the forces that drove FinTech growth in India and explain how public rails and private innovation interact. (Analyse)
  4. Evaluate the merits and challenges of FinTech. In your judgement, do the benefits outweigh the risks for rural India? Justify your answer. (Evaluate)
  5. Using the UPI ecosystem as a case, analyse the design choices that made it successful, the challenges it faces and the lessons for other FinTech services. (Analyse)
  6. Design a proposal for a FinTech service for Self Help Groups in the Nilgiris. Identify ecosystem partners, expected risks and governance controls, drawing on at least three Arthashastra principles. (Create)

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.html:
TermMeaning
FinTechTechnology-enabled innovation in financial services that creates new business models, products or processes.
EcosystemThe interconnected network of firms, institutions, regulators, investors and customers that delivers financial services.
TechFinA large technology company with existing data and customers that extends into financial services.
Digital bankingDelivery of a traditional bank's services through digital channels.
UnbundlingSeparation of a bundled bank service into specialised offerings by different firms.
RebundlingCombination of several services by one platform after it gains scale.
Co-opetitionA relationship in which firms both compete and cooperate.
Embedded financeFinancial services built into non-financial apps and websites.
Open bankingSharing of customer financial data with third parties through secure APIs and with consent.
CBDCCentral Bank Digital Currency, a digital form of sovereign money.
Digital divideThe gap between people who can and cannot access and use digital technology.
Systemic riskThe risk that failure in one part of the financial system spreads to others.
KoshaIn the Arthashastra, the treasury, regarded as the foundation of the state.
YogakshemaIn the Arthashastra, the welfare and security of the people.
SaptangaKautilya's theory of the seven elements of a state.
JAM trinityJan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar identity and Mobile phones, the base of India's digital finance.
NPCINational Payments Corporation of India, which operates retail payment systems such as UPI.
